meta.title: Cursor vs ellul: editor and cloud agents, or sovereign workstation
meta.description: Cursor ships an editor, a CLI, and Cloud Agents. Ellul integrates Cursor's Agent SDK for chat and runs cursor-agent (plus Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) on a passkey-gated workstation you own.

hero.headline: Cursor's runtime, or yours.
hero.sub: Cursor's editor is unmatched, and as of 2026 they also ship a CLI and a Cloud Agent product. Ellul integrates Cursor's Agent SDK for chat and runs cursor-agent (alongside Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) on a workstation you own. The comparison is less about whether Cursor's agent can run elsewhere and more about which runtime envelope it runs inside.

cursor.ellulPitch: Anything that involves the agent working without you, on infrastructure you own. Overnight runs. Parallel agents from different vendors. Real-credential operations like git push and database migrations gated by your passkey, not Cursor's auth. Long refactors that take eight hours. Picking up a task on your phone in the subway. Cursor's Cloud Agents put work on Cursor's runtime; Ellul puts work on yours.
cursor.competitorPitch: Cursor's editing experience is unmatched in 2026. Inline completions, command-K, codebase indexing, and the agent panel are all the strongest in their category. The cursor-agent CLI brings the same loop to your terminal, and Cloud Agents (Cursor's hosted runtime) can keep running while you close your laptop. Stay entirely inside Cursor's ecosystem if it fits.
cursor.fundamentalDifference: Cursor sells the editor, the agent, and (increasingly) the runtime as one bundled stack. Ellul is the runtime under whichever agent you choose, including Cursor's. Ellul integrates Cursor's Agent SDK for the chat experience and pre-installs cursor-agent on every workstation, so you keep Cursor's editor and CLI but the agent process lives on infrastructure you control, with a passkey gate, parallel-agent peering, and model-agnostic BYOK across Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode in the same workstation.

where-agent-runs.ellul: Per-user VPS you own and control
where-agent-runs.competitor: Local (editor + CLI) or Cursor's hosted runtime (Cloud Agents)
where-agent-runs.note: Cursor's Cloud Agents run on Cursor-managed infrastructure; Ellul runs on a per-user VPS dedicated to you.

survives-lid-close.competitor: Yes via Cloud Agents; no for local editor / CLI sessions

parallel-multi-vendor.ellul: Yes (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode in one workstation; read-only peering between)

editor-experience.ellul: Browser file browser + terminal; pair with Cursor locally as the editor
editor-experience.competitor: The strongest native editor experience in the category

inline-completions.ellul: Through Cursor on your laptop, paired with Ellul as the runtime

privileged-action-gating.ellul: FIDO2 passkey, server-side enforced outside the agent process

credentials-location.ellul: Server-side vault, brokered to the agent per-call
credentials-location.competitor: Local machine (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, 1Password CLI) or Cursor-managed for Cloud Agents

cursor-sdk-integration.ellul: Yes (Ellul's chat surface speaks Cursor's ACP, so cursor-agent runs as a first-class adapter alongside other CLIs)
cursor-sdk-integration.competitor: Native to Cursor's products by definition

phone-approvals.ellul: Yes (chat, files, passkey approvals from any registered device)
phone-approvals.competitor: Limited (Cloud Agents have a web UI, no passkey gates)

verdict.headline: Cursor for the editor and the agent, Ellul for the runtime that owns the agent.
verdict.body: Most senior engineers we talk to pay for both. Cursor stays on your laptop as the editor; cursor-agent and any other CLI live on an Ellul workstation. Cursor's Cloud Agents are an option if you want to stay entirely inside their ecosystem; Ellul is the option if you want sovereignty over where the agent runs, multi-vendor agents in parallel, and a passkey gate the runtime enforces.

whenToUseCompetitor.editor-heavy-day: You spend 90%+ of your day in the editor with the agent doing inline assists.
whenToUseCompetitor.short-cycle: Your work is short-cycle: prompt, see result, accept, move on.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-extra-credentials: You don't need credentials beyond what already lives on your laptop.
whenToUseCompetitor.cursor-runtime-fine: You're happy with Cursor owning the agent's runtime (local or Cloud Agents).

whenToUseEllul.long-tasks-walk-away: You want to kick off a long task on infrastructure you own and walk away.
whenToUseEllul.parallel-multi-vendor: You want to run multiple agents in parallel: coding (Claude Code), reviewing (cursor-agent), documenting (OpenCode).
whenToUseEllul.real-infra-passkey: Your agent needs to touch real infrastructure (GitHub, Vercel, production databases) and you want those credentials gated by your passkey, not Cursor's auth.
whenToUseEllul.passkey-every-action: You want passkey approvals for every privileged action, enforced outside the agent process.
whenToUseEllul.keep-editor-swap-runtime: You want to keep your editor (Cursor or anything else) and only swap the runtime.

use-cursor-with-ellul.q: Can I use Cursor with Ellul together?
use-cursor-with-ellul.a: Yes. Many of our customers do. Cursor stays on your laptop as the editor; cursor-agent runs on Ellul as one of the agent CLIs in the workstation. Ellul's chat surface speaks Cursor's Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), so the integration is first-class. You keep the editor experience and gain a sovereign runtime.

about-cloud-agents.a: Cursor shipped Cloud Agents in 2026, where you push a conversation to Cursor's hosted runtime and it keeps running while you're away. The trade-off is whose runtime owns the work. Cloud Agents run on Cursor-managed infrastructure with Cursor-managed credentials. Ellul is the same shape of capability on a per-user VPS you own, with passkey-gated privileged actions and multi-agent peering.

pay-for-both.q: Why would I pay for both?
pay-for-both.a: Different jobs. Cursor is for inline assists at the keyboard and the strongest editor experience in the category. Ellul is for unattended runs on infrastructure you control, parallel agents from multiple vendors, and credential-touching operations gated outside the agent process. Most senior engineers we talk to pay for both.

ellul-inline-completions.a: No. Inline completions assume the agent is co-located with the editor on your machine. Ellul's agent lives on the server. If you want inline completions plus a sovereign runtime, you run Cursor on your laptop and Ellul on the server, and cursor-agent on Ellul handles the long-running work.

cursor-vs-ellul-security.q: Is Cursor more secure than Ellul?
cursor-vs-ellul-security.a: Different threat models. Cursor's local agent has the same OS-level access to your filesystem as you do: every credential file, every browser cookie, every SSH key. Cloud Agents move that to Cursor-managed infrastructure with Cursor-managed credentials. Ellul's agent runs in an isolated per-user VPS with credentials in a server-side vault, gated by a separate process the agent cannot ptrace into. If you want kernel-enforced isolation and passkey-gated privileged actions, the architectures aren't comparable.

meta.title: Claude Code vs ellul: local agent or persistent workstation
meta.description: Claude Code is Anthropic's coding-agent CLI that runs on your laptop. Ellul runs Claude Code (and Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) on a persistent cloud workstation that never closes.

hero.headline: The agent, and the place the agent lives.
hero.sub: Claude Code is the agent. Ellul is the computer the agent runs on. You can run Claude Code locally, or you can run it on Ellul: same agent, different home.

claude-code.ellulPitch: Claude Code on your laptop has an unsolvable problem: it stops when you close the lid. Anthropic's 'Remote Control' feature relays input from another device, but the session still lives on your laptop. Ellul moves the session itself onto a persistent workstation. Same agent. New home.
claude-code.competitorPitch: The agent itself. Anthropic's agent quality is exceptional: Claude Opus 4.7 leads Terminal-Bench 2.0 (~69%) and SWE-bench Verified in the high 80s, with strong code review and multi-step planning. Their CLI experience is clean. Their MCP integration is the deepest in the industry. Their permissions model is the most thoughtful per-action gating any local agent has.
claude-code.fundamentalDifference: Claude Code is one of the strongest coding agents in 2026. We default to it. The question is not Claude Code or Ellul. It's where you want Claude Code to live. On your laptop, where it stops when the lid closes? Or on Ellul, where it runs through the night?

where-agent-runs.competitor: Your laptop (or relay via Remote Control)

gate-bypass-protection.capability: Cannot bypass gate (gate enforced outside agent)
gate-bypass-protection.note: Claude Code's gate runs in the agent process; Ellul's gate runs separately.

total-monthly-pro.note: You're paying for the workstation, not for the agent.

verdict.headline: Same agent, different home. Use Claude Code on Ellul when the laptop's lid is the problem.
verdict.body: Anthropic ships a great agent. We ship the workstation that lets it run while you sleep. Bring your own Claude subscription. Ellul charges only for the computer.

whenToUseCompetitor.trying-claude-code: You're trying Claude Code for the first time and want to feel the agent quality without committing to a workstation.
whenToUseCompetitor.fast-bounded: Your work is fast and bounded: short cycles where the agent shouldn't outlive your editor.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-prod-credentials: You don't need to touch production credentials.

whenToUseEllul.keep-running-after-lid-close: You want Claude Code to keep working after you close your laptop.
whenToUseEllul.parallel-sessions-no-clash: You want to run two or three Claude Code sessions in parallel without ports clashing.
whenToUseEllul.safe-git-push-deploy: You want git push and deploy to be safe, gated by a passkey, with credentials never in the agent's process.
whenToUseEllul.switch-between-clis: You want to switch between Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor without changing your workstation.

byok-claude.q: Can I bring my own Claude Pro/Max subscription to Ellul?
byok-claude.a: Yes. Ellul is BYOK (bring your own key). Your Claude subscription is yours; Ellul charges only for the workstation.

remote-control-replace.a: No. Remote Control lets you send messages from another device into a Claude Code session. The session itself still lives on your laptop, and stops when your laptop sleeps. Ellul moves the session onto a server that never sleeps.

gate-vs-permissions.q: How is Ellul's gate different from Claude Code's permissions?
gate-vs-permissions.a: Claude Code's permissions are enforced inside the agent process. Strong by software-engineering standards, but bypassable in principle by anyone with code-edit access to the agent. Ellul's gate is enforced by a separate process the agent cannot read, attach to, or signal. The agent literally cannot exfiltrate credentials at the OS level, not just by convention.

cloud-claude-code.q: Will Anthropic ship a cloud Claude Code?
cloud-claude-code.a: They ship Claude Managed Agents on platform.claude.com, a managed agent product tied to Anthropic's cloud and model. Ellul is model-agnostic: same workstation runs Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. Different scope.

mcp-servers.a: Ellul runs MCP servers either locally inside the workstation or as long-lived server-side processes. Local MCPs that need GPU or persistent state actually work, because the workstation isn't being torn down every time you close the lid.

meta.title: Claude Code vs Cursor: where the agent should live
meta.description: Claude Code and Cursor compared head-to-head: agent quality, editor surface, and the question neither vendor wants you to ask. Where does the agent run when you close your laptop?

hero.headline: The agent vs the editor, and the place either of them lives.
hero.sub: Claude Code wins on agent quality. Cursor wins on editor polish. Both run on your laptop. Here is the head-to-head, and the third option neither sells.

claude-code-vs-cursor.ellulPitch: Claude Code on a workstation that doesn't sleep. Run multiple sessions in parallel, gate every privileged action behind a passkey, keep credentials out of the agent process. Bring your own Claude/Codex/Cursor CLI subscription. Ellul charges for the workstation, not the model.
claude-code-vs-cursor.competitorPitch: Cursor's editor experience is the best in the category in 2026. Inline completions are instant. Codebase indexing is deep. Command-K is reflexive after a week. If you spend ninety percent of your day in the editor, Cursor's surface is hard to beat.
claude-code-vs-cursor.fundamentalDifference: Claude Code is the agent. Cursor is the editor. Ellul is the computer the agent runs on. Most senior engineers we talk to use Claude Code for the model and Cursor for the keyboard, then run Claude Code on Ellul so the lid problem stops mattering.

agent-quality.ellul: Claude Code default; Codex / OpenCode optional
agent-quality.note: Independent of where the agent runs.

inline-completions.note: Inline completions assume the agent is co-located with the editor. Use Cursor on your laptop AND Ellul on the server; they compose.

credentials-location.ellul: Server vault, never in agent process

run-other-agents.capability: Run other agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode)
run-other-agents.note: Cursor's CLI works on Ellul too.

hobby.note: Cursor Pro is the default subscription tier.

verdict.headline: Use Cursor for inline editing on your laptop. Use Claude Code for the agent itself. Run Claude Code on Ellul so it survives the lid closing.
verdict.body: If you're forced to pick one, the answer in April 2026 is Cursor for short-cycle in-the-editor work, Claude Code for anything resembling an unattended run. The interesting question is whether you should be running either of them on a machine you carry around in a bag.

whenToUseCompetitor.editor-heavy-day: You spend 90%+ of your day in the editor with the agent doing inline assists.
whenToUseCompetitor.short-cycle: Your work is short-cycle: prompt, see result, accept, move on.
whenToUseCompetitor.best-inline-completions: You want the best inline-completion experience in the industry.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-extra-credentials: You don't need credentials beyond what already lives on your laptop.

whenToUseEllul.overnight-runs-laptop-closed: You want to run Claude Code (or Codex, or Cursor's CLI) overnight without your laptop staying open.
whenToUseEllul.parallel-sessions-no-clash: You want multiple parallel agent sessions without state collisions.
whenToUseEllul.real-infra-no-laptop: Your agent needs to touch real infrastructure (GitHub, Vercel, production databases) and you don't want those credentials on your laptop.
whenToUseEllul.passkey-gated-git-push: You want a passkey-gated git push and deploy that the agent literally cannot bypass.
whenToUseEllul.move-agent-keep-editor: You want to keep your favorite editor (Cursor or otherwise) and just move the agent off.

claude-code-vs-cursor-better.q: Is Claude Code better than Cursor?
claude-code-vs-cursor-better.a: Different products. Claude Code's agent quality leads in 2026: Claude Opus 4.7 sits at the top of Terminal-Bench 2.0 (~69%) and posts SWE-bench Verified in the high 80s, with deeper code review and more reliable multi-step planning. Cursor's editor surface is the best in the category: inline completions, command-K, codebase indexing. Most senior engineers we talk to use both.

run-claude-code-on-cursor.q: Can I run Claude Code on Cursor?
run-claude-code-on-cursor.a: Cursor and Claude Code coexist on your laptop. Cursor is the editor; Claude Code is a CLI you trigger from a terminal. They don't conflict, but they both run on your machine, which means they both stop when your laptop sleeps.

cursor-cloud-agent.q: Does Cursor have a cloud-agent product?
cursor-cloud-agent.a: Cursor shipped Cloud Agents and the cursor-agent CLI in 2026, plus a Cursor SDK for embedding the same runtime in other apps. Cloud Agents push a conversation to Cursor's hosted runtime so it keeps running while you close your laptop. Ellul's positioning sits next to that: same shape of capability on a per-user VPS you own, with passkey-gated privileged actions, multi-vendor agents in parallel (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode beside cursor-agent), and Cursor's Agent Communication Protocol integrated so the chat surface is first-class.

anthropic-cloud-claude-code.q: Does Anthropic have a cloud Claude Code?
anthropic-cloud-claude-code.a: Anthropic ships Claude Managed Agents on platform.claude.com and a 'Remote Control' feature in Claude Code that lets another device send messages into a session. Both still tie you to Anthropic's cloud and Anthropic's model. Ellul is model-agnostic: the same workstation runs Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor's CLI.

pay-for-both.q: Why would I pay for both Cursor and Ellul?
pay-for-both.a: Different jobs. Cursor is for inline assists at the keyboard. Ellul is for unattended work, parallel agents, and credential-touching operations. Cursor on your laptop and an agent on Ellul is the most common configuration we see.

cursor-more-secure-than-claude-code-on-e.q: Is Cursor more secure than Claude Code on Ellul?
cursor-more-secure-than-claude-code-on-e.a: No. Cursor's agent has the same OS-level access to your filesystem as you do: every credential file, every browser cookie, every SSH key. Ellul's agent runs in an isolated sandbox with credentials in a server-side vault, gated by a separate process the agent cannot read or attach to. Threat model is fundamentally different.

meta.title: GitHub Codespaces vs ellul: dev env or agent home
meta.description: GitHub Codespaces was built for humans writing code in a browser. Ellul is built for AI agents: gated, parallel, agent-native. The shape of the product follows from who it's for.

hero.headline: Built for humans, or built for agents.
hero.sub: GitHub Codespaces is the canonical cloud dev environment for humans typing code in a browser. Ellul is built for agents: gated, parallel, agent-native. The shape of the product follows from who it's for.

codespaces.ellulPitch: Anything where the agent is doing the work and the human is approving. Codespaces has no concept of an agent that runs unattended, no FIDO2 gate, no per-agent isolation, no peering primitive. We were built for the agent first.
codespaces.competitorPitch: GitHub-native. Free tier. Tight integration with the GitHub ecosystem. If you're a human writing code in a browser and your work lives in GitHub, Codespaces is excellent.
codespaces.fundamentalDifference: Codespaces' design assumption: a human is in the editor, the agent (Copilot) helps them. Ellul's: an agent is in the workstation, the human approves the dangerous parts. Once you change who is at the keyboard, almost every product decision changes: gating, parallelism, peering, credential handling.

bring-any-agent.capability: Bring any agent (Claude, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode)

verdict.headline: Codespaces is for humans typing in a browser. Ellul is for the agent doing the work.
verdict.body: If your agent usage is light Copilot inline assists, Codespaces' free tier is a great deal. If you want unattended overnight runs, multiple parallel agents, and gated production access, that's a different shape of product.

whenToUseCompetitor.human-typing-browser: You're a human typing code in a browser-based VS Code.
whenToUseCompetitor.github-standardized: Your team standardizes on GitHub for everything.
whenToUseCompetitor.free-tier-occasional: You want a free tier for occasional cloud work.
whenToUseCompetitor.light-copilot-assists: Your agent usage is light Copilot inline assists.

whenToUseEllul.agent-not-at-keyboard: You want an agent to do the work while you're not at the keyboard.
whenToUseEllul.multi-parallel-each-workstation: You want multiple agents in parallel, each with its own workstation.
whenToUseEllul.passkey-gates-on-actions: You want passkey gates on git push and deploys.
whenToUseEllul.choose-agent-not-copilot: You want to choose your agent (Claude, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) without being tied to Copilot.

claude-code-or-cursor-in-codespace.q: Why can't I just run Claude Code or Cursor in a Codespace?
claude-code-or-cursor-in-codespace.a: You can. People do. The problem is structural: Codespaces auto-suspend on idle, there's no gate model for the agent's privileged actions, there's no peering primitive, and credentials live in your GitHub-attached environment with no per-action approval. It works for short sessions; for unattended overnight runs it's painful.

ellul-free-tier.q: Does Ellul have a free tier?
ellul-free-tier.a: No. We've found that free tiers attract a different ICP than the senior engineers we serve. We may add one later.

codespaces-cheaper-occasional.q: Is Codespaces cheaper for occasional use?
codespaces-cheaper-occasional.a: Yes. 60 free hours/month plus pay-as-you-go beats $20/month flat if you Codespace once a week. Ellul is for daily-driver use where the workstation is always on.

github-agent-first-codespace.q: Will GitHub ship an agent-first Codespace?
github-agent-first-codespace.a: They've shipped agent features tied to Copilot. Whether that converges to a real agent workstation with gating and peering remains to be seen. Until then Ellul is years ahead on those specific axes.

codespaces-and-ellul-together.q: Can I use Codespaces and Ellul together?
codespaces-and-ellul-together.a: Yes; they don't conflict. Use Codespaces for in-the-browser human coding, use Ellul for unattended agent runs. The pricing structures are independent.

meta.title: Daytona vs ellul: workspace primitive or product
meta.description: Daytona is a workspace primitive that targets platform engineers building developer environments. Ellul is the assembled, opinionated agent workstation that uses workspace primitives internally.

hero.headline: A primitive, or the product built on it.
hero.sub: Daytona's docs target platform engineers building developer environments. Ellul is the assembled product an engineer signs up for. Different audiences.

daytona.ellulPitch: Daytona has a solid foundation but no agent-specific UX, no passkey gating, no peering primitive, no integrations. We've built the layer above. A senior engineer signs up for Ellul and is productive in five minutes.
daytona.competitorPitch: Stateful workspaces with unlimited persistence and a clean SDK. Strong primitive for platform engineers. Open-source posture is honest.
daytona.fundamentalDifference: Daytona is to dev environments what Kubernetes is to containers: a powerful primitive that requires assembly. Ellul is the assembled experience: chat, gates, peering, integrations. If you have a platform team and want to build your own internal agent platform, Daytona is sensible. If you want to use an agent today, Ellul is the answer.

total-individual.competitor: Cloud + ops time, typically more for individuals

verdict.headline: Daytona for platform teams; Ellul for individual senior engineers.
verdict.body: If your job is to build a developer platform, Daytona is a sensible primitive. If your job is to ship code with an agent, Ellul is the assembled product you sign up for.

whenToUseCompetitor.platform-team-internal: You have a platform team and you want to build an internal developer platform.
whenToUseCompetitor.workspace-primitives-extend: You need workspace primitives you can extend yourself.
whenToUseCompetitor.oss-priority-time-control: Your priority is open source and you'll trade time for control.

whenToUseEllul.use-agent-not-build-platform: You want to use an agent, not build a platform.
whenToUseEllul.gates-peering-integrations-oob: You want passkey gates, peering, and integrations out of the box.
whenToUseEllul.productive-minutes-not-weeks: You want to be productive in minutes, not weeks.

build-ellul-on-daytona.q: Could I build Ellul on Daytona?
build-ellul-on-daytona.a: In principle, yes. Daytona provides the workspace primitive. Ellul is roughly 18 months of additional product engineering: chat, gates, peering, integrations, identity, billing. We've already built it.

ellul-uses-daytona.q: Does Ellul use Daytona under the hood?
ellul-uses-daytona.a: No. Our sandboxes use a different stack with a security model that requires the gate to be enforced outside the agent process, which off-the-shelf workspace primitives don't ship with.

daytona-oss-story.a: We respect it. Open-source workspace primitives are valuable. They live one layer below where Ellul operates. The full product Ellul ships is not yet open source.

daytona-cheaper.a: Daytona is free if you self-host, plus the cost of the cloud you run it on. The total cost of operating a self-hosted Daytona workspace plus building the agent product on top usually exceeds Ellul's $20 to $50 per month for individual engineers.

daytona-passkey-gate.q: Does Daytona have a passkey gate?
daytona-passkey-gate.a: No. Daytona provides workspace primitives. Authorization and gating are something you assemble on top. Ellul ships an opinionated FIDO2-enforced gate that's part of the product.

meta.title: E2B vs ellul: ephemeral execution or persistent agent
meta.description: E2B provides ephemeral code-execution sandboxes (capped at 24 hours on Pro) via Firecracker microVMs. Ellul is a persistent agent workstation that lasts as long as your account.

hero.headline: Ephemeral code execution, or persistent agent work.
hero.sub: E2B is for short bursts of code execution inside a sandbox. Ellul is for an agent that lives on a workstation indefinitely. Different problems.

e2b.ellulPitch: Persistence. An Ellul workstation is yours for the duration of your account. Your installed packages, your config, your in-progress branches stay where you left them. E2B sandboxes don't.
e2b.competitorPitch: Firecracker microVMs with strong isolation. Solid SDK for building 'run user code in a sandbox' features. The right primitive for code interpreters and untrusted-input scenarios.
e2b.fundamentalDifference: E2B sandboxes are ephemeral by design: they exist for the duration of a code-execution call, capped at 24 hours on Pro. Ellul workstations are persistent by design: they exist until you cancel your subscription. If you're building an LLM app that runs untrusted code, use E2B. If you're an engineer who wants an always-on agent, use Ellul.

heavy-unattended.competitor: Per-second wins for bursty / short-lived workloads

verdict.headline: E2B for code interpreters. Ellul for an engineer's daily-driver agent workstation.
verdict.body: Some products use both: E2B for code interpreters and Ellul for the engineering workstation that builds them. They aren't substitutes; they're tools at different layers of the stack.

whenToUseCompetitor.untrusted-user-code: You're building an LLM app that needs to run untrusted user code.
whenToUseCompetitor.seconds-to-minutes: Your sandboxes live for seconds to minutes, not hours.
whenToUseCompetitor.per-second-billing: You want per-second billing tied to actual usage.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-state-persistence: You don't need state to survive between sandbox lifetimes.

whenToUseEllul.agent-not-sdk: You're an engineer who wants an agent, not an SDK.
whenToUseEllul.hours-or-days-context: Your agent needs hours or days of context, not seconds.
whenToUseEllul.persistent-home-deps: You want a persistent home for installed packages, branches, and in-progress work.
whenToUseEllul.passkey-gated-git-push: You want passkey-gated git push and deploys.

e2b-vs-ellul.a: They solve different problems. E2B is the right answer for ephemeral code execution. Ellul is the right answer for persistent agent work. Some products use both: E2B for code interpreters and Ellul for the engineering workstation that builds them.

e2b-as-workstation.q: Could I use E2B as my agent's workstation?
e2b-as-workstation.a: It would work for short tasks. For anything taking longer than the sandbox cap (24h on Pro), the sandbox dies and the agent's work goes with it. Ellul exists because that ceiling is too low for serious unattended work.

e2b-persistence.a: E2B's Pro plan supports sessions up to 24 hours. After that the sandbox tears down. State has to be exfiltrated and re-loaded, which is fine for code interpreters and painful for agents.

pricing-comparison.a: If your sandbox usage is bursty (lots of short sessions), E2B's per-second pricing is cheaper. If you're keeping an agent alive for hours every day, Ellul's flat monthly wins.

e2b-passkey-gating.a: No. E2B is sandbox infrastructure; gating is something you build at the application layer. Ellul ships a FIDO2-enforced gate as a first-class part of the product.

competitor.tagline: Stateful sandboxes for AI coding agents

meta.title: Sprites vs ellul: sandbox infrastructure or product
meta.description: Sprites.dev provides stateful sandboxes for AI coding agents on Firecracker microVMs. Ellul is the assembled product (chat, file browser, gates, integrations) built on top of stateful sandboxes.

hero.headline: Sandbox infrastructure, or the product on top of it.
hero.sub: Sprites.dev provides stateful sandboxes other companies build on. Ellul is the product an engineer signs up for. Both have a place; they live at different layers.

sprites.ellulPitch: We are the assembled experience. Chat surface. File browser. Live preview. Passkey gates. Composition primitive. GitHub/Vercel/Neon/Supabase integrations. A senior engineer can sign up for Ellul and have an agent running in five minutes. They don't have to assemble it themselves.
sprites.competitorPitch: Firecracker microVMs with checkpoint and rollback on fast NVMe. Genuine 'unlimited persistence.' Strong primitive for builders who need sandbox-as-a-service. Their docs are clean and their pricing is honest.
sprites.fundamentalDifference: Sprites is infrastructure. Ellul is a product. If you're building an AI coding tool and need stateful sandboxes as a primitive, Sprites is the right call. If you're a senior engineer who wants an always-on workstation for your agent, Ellul is what you sign up for. The two are complementary.

builtin-ux.note: Sprites: you build it. Ellul: ships with it.

high-volume.competitor: Per-second pricing wins for thousands of short-lived sandboxes

verdict.headline: Different layers of the stack: Sprites is infrastructure, Ellul is the product.
verdict.body: Use Sprites if you're building a coding-agent product and need sandbox primitives. Use Ellul if you're a senior engineer who wants to use an agent today, not assemble one over six months.

whenToUseCompetitor.building-coding-agent: You're building a coding agent product and need stateful sandboxes as infrastructure.
whenToUseCompetitor.own-ux-from-scratch: You want to own the entire user experience from scratch.
whenToUseCompetitor.granular-per-second: You need granular per-second pricing for a high-volume sandbox workload.

whenToUseEllul.use-agent-not-build: You're a senior engineer who wants to use an agent, not build one.

whenToUseEllul.passkey-without-writing-gate: You want passkey-gated privileged actions without writing the gate yourself.
whenToUseEllul.flat-monthly: You want a flat monthly price.

sprites-build-ellul-like.q: Could Sprites.dev be used to build something like Ellul?
sprites-build-ellul-like.a: In principle, yes. Sprites is infrastructure. The full product (chat, files, gates, peering, integrations) is roughly 18 months of engineering on top. We've already built it.

ellul-uses-sprites.q: Does Ellul use Sprites under the hood?
ellul-uses-sprites.a: No. Our sandboxes are built on a different stack with a custom security model. Passkey gating is enforced by a separate process the agent cannot read or attach to, which requires more than what an off-the-shelf sandbox provides.

sprites-cheaper-high-volume.q: Is Sprites cheaper for high-volume agent runs?
sprites-cheaper-high-volume.a: If you're spinning up thousands of short-lived sandboxes per day, Sprites' per-second pricing wins. If you're a senior engineer running a few persistent workstations, our flat monthly is usually cheaper.

sprites-passkey-gating.a: No. Sprites provides sandbox primitives. Gating is something you build on top, and getting it right is hard, because the gate has to be enforced outside the agent process to be meaningful.

composition-primitive.a: Read-only peering between agents (letting one agent see another's source without writing) is a property of the orchestration layer, not the sandbox layer. Sprites doesn't ship it. Ellul does.

why-comparison-on-site.q: Why is this comparison even on this site?

base44-after-wix.a: Base44 continues to ship as a Wix property. The naming and bundling have shifted with successive Wix releases; for current details, the Base44 product page is the source of truth.

lovable-bolt-v0.a: All in the same prompt-to-app builder category, with different polish and different model stacks. hero.headline: Prompt-to-app, or agent's runtime.
hero.sub: Bolt is a strong prompt-to-running-app product on top of StackBlitz's WebContainer tech. Ellul is the persistent computer an engineer's AI agent lives on. They serve different users. Here's where each one wins.

bolt.ellulPitch: Engineering on a real codebase: your agent, your model, your tools, your repo. Long-running tasks, parallel agents, real credentials gated by a passkey, persistent workstation between sessions. Ellul is the runtime; you bring whichever agent CLI suits the job.

Ellul is the runtime under your agent: you bring the editor, the agent, the model, the deploy target. bolt-coding-agent-like-claude.q: Is Bolt a coding agent like Claude Code?
bolt-coding-agent-like-claude.a: Different shape. Bolt is a prompt-to-app product; the agent is implicit. Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex are coding agents you keep using across projects, with their own CLI and model contracts. Ellul is the runtime under those coding agents.

export-bolt-to-ellul.q: Can I export from Bolt to Ellul?
export-bolt-to-ellul.a: Yes. Bolt supports GitHub export. Once you have the repo, you can clone it onto an Ellul workstation and continue with Cursor, Claude Code, or your preferred agent. The 'graduate from prompt-builder to engineer-with-agent' path is a common one.

what-is-webcontainer.q: What's WebContainer and why does it matter?
what-is-webcontainer.a: StackBlitz built WebContainer, a Node.js runtime that runs inside the browser via WebAssembly. It's a real strength for Bolt: 'preview' is actual code execution in the browser, not a server round-trip. It does not generalize to all environments (no Docker, limited native modules) but for the apps Bolt targets, it's a uniquely fast loop.

bolt-vs-other-builders.q: Bolt vs Lovable vs v0 vs Base44: are they all the same?
bolt-vs-other-builders.a: All in the same prompt-to-app builder category, with different polish and different model stacks. Bolt's WebContainer runtime is its differentiator; Lovable's React quality is its; v0's design fidelity is its; Base44's full-stack scope is its. Ellul is structurally orthogonal to all four.

bolt-graduates-to-real-product.q: What if my Bolt prototype graduates into a real product?
bolt-graduates-to-real-product.a: Export to GitHub, clone onto an Ellul workstation, point your preferred agent CLI at the repo. The agent now lives on a persistent server, can run unattended, has passkey-gated production access, and works alongside other agents you spin up.

hero.headline: A managed engineer, or your agent's workstation.
hero.sub: Devin is Cognition's product: hand it a task, it works in their sandbox, you get a PR. Ellul is the runtime under your own agent (your Claude Code, your Cursor, your Codex) on a persistent workstation that's yours. Different commitments, different shapes.

devin.ellulPitch: Engineering work where you keep your existing agent CLI, your model contract, your codebase ownership, and your deploy target. Ellul is the runtime; you choose the agent and the model. Flat pricing, persistent workstation, parallel-capable, passkey-gated.
devin.competitorPitch: If you want a fully managed product where Cognition's agent does the engineering, picks the model, runs the sandbox, and produces a PR with minimal handholding, Devin is the highest-profile entry in that category. The product is opinionated end-to-end and well-funded.
devin.fundamentalDifference: Devin is the agent and the runtime, sold together as a managed product. Ellul is the runtime under your agent: your existing Claude Code or Cursor CLI on a persistent workstation, with your credentials and your tools. Devin is high-end SaaS; Ellul is infrastructure. verdict.body: If you specifically want a managed product where Cognition's agent does the work and you don't want to operate any infrastructure, Devin is in your category. If you want your existing Cursor / Claude Code / Codex agent on a persistent workstation, with your credentials, your model, and your repo, Ellul is in your category. Most engineers we talk to who evaluate both don't actually choose between them; they end up with their own agent on Ellul because that's the shape of their existing workflow.

whenToUseCompetitor.managed-bundled: You want a fully managed product where the agent and the runtime are bundled.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-existing-cli: You don't have an existing agent CLI you want to keep using.
whenToUseCompetitor.ok-with-pricing: You're fine with the per-task / high-tier pricing model.

whenToUseEllul.flat-rate-pricing: You want flat-rate pricing rather than per-task or high-tier subscriptions.
whenToUseEllul.real-credential-passkey: Your agent needs real-credential operations gated by your passkey.
whenToUseEllul.parallel-structural-isolation: You want parallel agents with structural isolation.

devin-on-ellul.q: Can I run Devin on Ellul?
devin-on-ellul.a: Devin is a managed product; it doesn't ship as a CLI you install on your own infrastructure. So no: you'd run Devin on Cognition's cloud and your other agents (Claude Code, Cursor's CLI, etc.) on Ellul.

devin-autonomy-vs-claude.q: Is Devin's autonomy more advanced than Claude Code on Ellul?
devin-autonomy-vs-claude.a: Hard to say categorically. Devin is opinionated about the loop and the model; Claude Code on Ellul is composable, so the agent's autonomy is whatever your model and your prompts produce. The decision usually comes down to whether you want a packaged product (Devin) or a runtime you can shape (Ellul).

devin-pricing.a: Devin 2.0 launched in April 2025 with a Core plan starting at $20/mo, billed pay-as-you-go at roughly $2.25 per Agent Compute Unit (about 15 minutes of agent work). Higher Pro and Max tiers exist for heavier individual usage; team and enterprise plans are above. Ellul is $20/mo Hobby and $50/mo Pro flat, plus whatever model API you're paying directly. The two products price for very different commercial shapes.

cognition-windsurf.q: Does Cognition's acquisition of Windsurf change anything?
cognition-windsurf.a: Cognition acquired Windsurf in 2025. The two products coexist with different deployment models: Devin is managed-cloud, Windsurf is a local IDE. From an Ellul perspective the change is mostly irrelevant. We run agent CLIs from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Cursor, Cognition, or anyone else, and the runtime stays the same.

devin-safer-than-claude-on-ellul.q: Is Devin safer than running Claude Code on Ellul?
devin-safer-than-claude-on-ellul.a: Safer along different axes. Devin's safety is 'we run the agent in our sandbox and curate what it can do.' Ellul's safety is 'kernel-level isolation per agent, passkey-gated privileged actions, credentials never in the agent process.' For real-credential engineering, Ellul's structural model is meaningfully harder to attack; for end-to-end task autonomy on bounded tickets, Devin's curated sandbox is a different reasonable choice.

is-manus-coding-agent.a: It can write code, but it's a generalist agent: research, reports, document synthesis, one-shot tasks. Most coding-engineer workflows want their own agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) running in their own codebase, which is the gap Ellul fills.

manus-and-ellul-together.q: Can I use Manus and Ellul together?

manus-codebase-integration.q: Does Manus integrate with my codebase?

manus-cheaper-ellul.a: It depends on usage. Manus's headline tier is in the same range as Ellul's Pro plan, but Manus tiers include task credits, so heavy usage adds up quickly. Ellul's pricing is flat. Your bill doesn't change with how hard your agent works.

data-sovereignty.a: Manus runs your tasks in their cloud, in their region, on their infrastructure. Ellul provisions your workstation in a region you choose, with LUKS-encrypted persistent storage and credentials that never leave your VPS. If your work is governed by data-handling rules that don't permit a managed third-party sandbox, Ellul is structurally easier to defend.

hero.headline: Generalist cloud IDE, or focused agent workstation.
hero.sub: Replit's been the cloud IDE since 2016 and now bundles Replit Agent plus deploy. Ellul is purpose-built for an engineer's AI agent: isolated, passkey-gated, model-agnostic. Different shapes, different users; here's where each one wins.

replit.ellulPitch: Engineering work where you bring your own agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode), keep your model contract direct with the model provider, and need real-credential operations gated by your passkey. Ellul is the runtime; you choose the agent, the model, and the deploy target.
replit.competitorPitch: Replit's broad reach, integrated hosting, education tier, and built-in Replit Agent give it an unusually low time-to-running-app for a wide range of users. If you want one product that does IDE, agent, and hosting in a single subscription, and you're fine with Replit's model and runtime choices, Replit is hard to beat for that bundle.
replit.fundamentalDifference: Replit bundles IDE, agent, and hosting into one product, optimized for breadth (learners through prosumers). Ellul unbundles those: it is the agent's runtime and nothing else, optimized for professional engineers running their own agent CLI in their own repo. The two products overlap in the keyword 'cloud development environment' and diverge from there.

byoa.ellul: Any CLI: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode

always-on-agent.competitor: Replit Agent runs as a session; not always-on by default

privileged-action-gating.competitor: Standard auth; no per-action passkey gate

credentials-location.ellul: Server vault, never in agent process

parallel-agents.competitor: Multiple Replit projects, no cross-project peering primitive

hosting-deployment.ellul: Deploy anywhere (Vercel, Fly, Railway, your infra)

editor-experience.ellul: Browser file browser + terminal; pair with your IDE locally

phone-approvals.ellul: Yes (chat, files, approvals from any device)

verdict.headline: Replit for the bundle; Ellul for the engineer who wants control of the runtime.
verdict.body: Replit is the right answer if you want IDE + agent + hosting in one subscription and you're fine with their stack. Ellul is the right answer if you're a professional engineer who wants to keep your existing agent CLI and model, host where you choose, and gate privileged actions with a passkey. They overlap on the keyword 'cloud dev environment' and diverge sharply on user shape and runtime model.

whenToUseCompetitor.bundle-ide-agent-hosting: You want one product for IDE, agent, and hosting.
whenToUseCompetitor.education-multiplayer: You teach or learn in Replit's education tier and the multiplayer / share-by-link features matter.
whenToUseCompetitor.replit-stack-ok: You're fine with Replit's model and runtime choices.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-passkey-byok-needed: Your work doesn't require per-action passkey gating or BYOK on a specific agent CLI.

whenToUseEllul.keep-existing-cli: You want to keep using Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or OpenCode as the agent.
whenToUseEllul.real-prod-credentials-passkey: Your agent needs to touch real production credentials, gated by passkey.
whenToUseEllul.flat-rate-pricing: You want flat-rate pricing and predictable bills.
whenToUseEllul.parallel-structural-isolation: You want parallel agents with structural isolation.
whenToUseEllul.deploy-elsewhere: You deploy your apps elsewhere (Vercel, Fly, Railway, your infra).

replit-agent-with-ellul.q: Can I use Replit Agent with Ellul?
replit-agent-with-ellul.a: Replit Agent is tightly bundled with Replit's runtime; it doesn't ship as a standalone CLI you can run on another host. If you want an agent on Ellul, the practical agents are Claude Code, Cursor's Agent CLI, Codex, and OpenCode, all of which run on Ellul.

replit-pricing-comparable.a: Roughly. Replit Core dropped to $20/mo (from $25) in February 2026, and Replit Pro at $100/mo replaced the old Teams plan in the same reshuffle. Ellul is $20/mo Hobby and $50/mo Pro. The thing that bundles differently is hosting: Replit Deployments are inside the same subscription; on Ellul, deploys go wherever you choose, which is sometimes free and sometimes a separate bill.

ellul-isolation-vs-replit.q: How does Ellul's isolation differ from Replit's?
ellul-isolation-vs-replit.a: Replit runs each project in a managed container on shared infrastructure. Ellul provisions a per-user VPS with kernel-level isolation: separate user, mount and PID namespaces, LUKS-encrypted storage, and a shield process that the agent cannot ptrace into. The threat model is meaningfully different.

ellul-replaces-replit.a: If you're a professional engineer and you specifically want an agent's runtime, yes. If you're a learner, hobbyist, or someone who wants the IDE-plus-hosting bundle, Replit is shaped for that and Ellul is not.

replit-agent-v2.q: What about Replit Agent v2 / Ghostwriter?
replit-agent-v2.a: Replit ships continuous improvements to its agent. The two-year-out comparison may narrow if Replit ships per-action gating, model-agnostic agent CLI support, and per-tenant kernel isolation. As of April 2026, the runtime model is still 'managed Replit container,' which is structurally different from Ellul's 'per-tenant VPS with shield.'

competitor.tagline: Cascade agent inside a VS Code fork on your laptop

meta.title: Windsurf vs ellul: agentic editor or persistent agent
meta.description: Windsurf is a VS Code fork with the Cascade agent built in. Ellul is the persistent workstation that agent can live on: no lid problem, parallel agents, passkey-gated production access.

hero.headline: Editor with an agent, or computer for the agent.
hero.sub: Windsurf bundles a Cascade agent into a polished VS Code fork. Ellul is upstream of that: the persistent workstation an agent lives on, regardless of which editor you use to talk to it. They are not the same product.

windsurf.ellulPitch: Anything where the agent's runtime matters: overnight runs, parallel agents on the same problem, real-credential operations, multi-day refactors, phone-as-keyboard for approvals while you're away. The thing Windsurf doesn't address is the runtime. The agent still lives on your laptop and inherits your laptop's lifecycle and credentials.
windsurf.competitorPitch: Windsurf's Cascade agent and Cascade Memories give it a strong inline experience with an opinionated editor. If your work is keyboard-bound and short-cycle, the in-editor flow is hard to beat, particularly for engineers who want a Cursor-style experience under different ownership and pricing.
windsurf.fundamentalDifference: Windsurf is the editor with the agent baked in. Ellul is the computer that agent runs on. They compose: keep Windsurf as your editor, point its Cascade-CLI workflows at an Ellul workstation so the agent doesn't share your laptop's lid, credentials, or single-process bottleneck.

parallel-agents.competitor: One Cascade session at a time

credentials-location.ellul: Server vault, never in agent process

editor-base-source.ellul: Editor-agnostic (Cursor, Claude Code, OpenCode, Codex all work)

verdict.headline: Windsurf for the editor; Ellul for the agent's runtime. Compose them.
verdict.body: If you like Windsurf's in-editor flow, keep using it. Move the heavy agent work (overnight runs, parallel agents, anything that touches production) onto an Ellul workstation. They solve different problems and stack cleanly.

whenToUseCompetitor.cursor-style-codeium-stack: You want a Cursor-style editor under different ownership and prefer Codeium's model stack.
whenToUseCompetitor.short-cycle-keyboard-bound: Your work is short-cycle, in-editor, and keyboard-bound.
whenToUseCompetitor.no-unattended-runs: You don't run agents unattended, and your credentials live happily on your laptop.
whenToUseCompetitor.opinionated-editor-builtin-agent: You want an opinionated editor with a built-in agent rather than composing your own stack.

whenToUseEllul.kick-off-and-walk-away: You want to kick off a long task and walk away from the keyboard.
whenToUseEllul.parallel-coding-reviewing-documenting: You want multiple agents in parallel: coding, reviewing, documenting.
whenToUseEllul.real-creds-not-on-laptop: Your agent needs real credentials (GitHub, Vercel, production DB) and you don't want them on your laptop.
whenToUseEllul.approve-from-phone: You want to approve actions from a phone.
whenToUseEllul.tired-of-laptop-stopping: You're tired of long jobs stopping when you close the lid.

windsurf-with-ellul.q: Can I use Windsurf with Ellul?
windsurf-with-ellul.a: Yes. Windsurf stays where it is, on your laptop, for the inline editor flow. Whichever agent CLI you prefer (Claude Code, Cursor's Agent CLI, Codex, OpenCode) points at an Ellul workstation so the agent itself runs on a persistent server. You keep the editor; the agent moves.

windsurf-teams-instead.q: Why not just buy Windsurf Teams?
windsurf-teams-instead.a: Windsurf Teams gives you better usage on Cascade and team features inside the editor. It does not give you a place for the agent to run when you close the laptop, parallel-agent peering, or passkey-gated production access. Those are runtime concerns; Windsurf is an editor.

cascade-vs-composer.q: Does Windsurf's Cascade agent work as well as Cursor's Composer?
cascade-vs-composer.a: Both have improved sharply through 2025 and 2026. Day-to-day, most reviews call it a near-tie on editor agent quality, with each ahead in different micro-cases. The decision between them is rarely about agent quality and usually about ecosystem preference (model stack, pricing, ownership).

windsurf-cloud-product.q: Will Windsurf launch a cloud product?
windsurf-cloud-product.a: Possible. Codeium's lineage is in self-hosted enterprise inference, and they've experimented with cloud workspaces. If Windsurf ships a competing always-on, parallel-agent, passkey-gated workstation, the comparison will narrow. Until then, Windsurf is local-first and Ellul is the runtime layer.

cognition-acquisition-relevant.q: Is the Cognition acquisition relevant here?
cognition-acquisition-relevant.a: Cognition (the company behind Devin) acquired Windsurf in 2025. It changed Windsurf's ownership and roadmap, not its architecture: Windsurf is still a local-first VS Code fork. Devin and Windsurf are still distinct products with different deployment models.
